prize_parts.citation: for a visionary, densely patterned prose, rooted in poetry, that turns memory, the body and dream into an encyclopedic metaphysical architecture

statement.case_for: Cărtărescu keeps my first place after reconsideration. Public knowledge supports an unmistakable voice and a formal project of unusual scale: Blinding (the opening volume of the Orbitor trilogy) and Solenoid build large structures in which memory, the body, dream and metaphysical speculation form one imaginative whole, with a poetic origin that shapes the imagery. The achievement lies in how the structure is built and sustained across volumes, not in scale alone. The work shows imaginative and intellectual depth, linguistic ambition and a body of work that has had time to be absorbed critically. That seems to me a strong fit with the criteria of voice, formal achievement, sustained quality and depth. I treat the fact that the colleagues' openings converge on this candidate as no evidence of merit. I weigh the work against the other shortlisted oeuvres, in particular Adonis, whose case I regard as very serious.
statement.case_against: My strongest reservation is that I cannot separate the achievement of the Romanian prose from the effect of translation. The claim rests on long, intricate sentences and rhythm that translation may inflate or blur. A related concern, raised in Carlberg's opening, is that imagery and motifs recur across the large volumes. That may be elaboration of a single mode rather than deepening, and some volumes may reward ambition more than finished execution. My knowledge of the poetry and early prose is thinner than of the major novels. I also see a possible argument that the claim for Adonis is more consequential for a language as a whole, and I take it seriously.

responses.point: Carlberg ranks Adonis first for a sustained remaking of Arabic poetic language through myth, fragmentation and dialogue with inherited forms. She also notes that Cărtărescu's imagery can be repetitive across volumes and that the quality of translation of the long novels is hard to judge.
responses.response: I agree on the literary weight of Adonis and ranked him second for the same reasons: formal and linguistic renewal of a tradition, plus a coherent essayistic counterpart. Her point about repetition in Cărtărescu is fair and is my main internal reservation, and I cannot rule it out from translation. I would qualify it, though. Recurrence of motifs in Solenoid and the Orbitor books appears to be part of a deliberate architecture and is not simple repetition. The translation caveat applies to both candidates, but it is sharper for poetry, whose claim lies in prosody and the relation to classical forms. That leaves me least able to verify the very ground on which the case for Adonis rests. That is a limit on my judgment and not a mark against him.

responses.point: Sward places Adonis first, centering the renewal of Arabic poetry, and warns that the weight of his critical prose could pull a citation away from the poetry. She places Cărtărescu second, citing the construction of an inner cosmos in prose and formal control over large structures.
responses.response: I share her concern about the citation. If Adonis were chosen, it should rest on the poetic achievement, with the essays as a companion, and not on political positions or the breadth of the critical writing. Her description of Cărtărescu as formally controlling very large structures is close to my own reason for ranking him first. Where we differ is on the weighting: I find that the sustained architecture across several large works is a somewhat stronger demonstration of the sustained-quality criterion than I can establish for poetry through translation. I hold that as a judgment under uncertainty. I do not think the case for Adonis is weak, and my own ranking puts him second.

responses.point: Mattson ranks Pierre Michon second, arguing that his compressed, syntactically exacting prose achieves depth through concentration rather than volume, though she grants that modest breadth may weigh against him on significance across a body of work.
responses.response: I ranked Michon eighth, and I take her point seriously: concentration is a legitimate form of achievement, and Small Lives and The Eleven are known for the exacting language she describes. My reservation is the one she names herself. The corpus is slender, the effect lies largely in French syntax that translation reduces, and I find it hard to establish breadth of significance across the oeuvre. I cannot say her argument has moved my ranking much, but it makes me less confident that a small corpus should count against him. I would want colleagues who read French directly to say whether the later work extends the method or repeats it.

responses.point: Sem-Sandberg ranks Cărtărescu first but advises that any citation be anchored in the prose project and not overstate the poetry. He also questions whether the mass and recurring motifs amount to development or elaboration of a single mode.
responses.response: I agree with the citation point and have drawn the proposed wording accordingly. It names the prose architecture as the achievement and mentions poetry only as the root of the imagery. His question about development versus elaboration is the strongest internal challenge to my first place. I think Solenoid suggests ambition extended rather than repeated, but I base that on reception and translation and cannot demonstrate it textually. I would welcome other members' views on how the later novels relate to the Orbitor books.

uncertainties: How much of Cărtărescu's stylistic achievement belongs to the Romanian original rather than to the translations on which my assessment relies.
Whether the recurrence of motifs across the large novels is development or elaboration of one mode.
The quality of the poetry and early prose relative to the major novels, which I know less well.
The weight of Adonis's poetic innovation against the translation limits on my ability to judge Arabic prosody.
Whether the oeuvre of Alexis Wright is large enough for the sustained-quality criterion, given the small number of major novels.
I have not independently verified any source text, and my knowledge rests on general public knowledge and the shortlist descriptions.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile. The profile records no relationship with any shortlisted writer, and my own literary practice is context only and does not bear on this preference.
